title: Hits in the Last Five Minutes
statement:
Build a counter for page hits that can tell how many hits arrived during the last five minutes.

  • HitWindow() creates an empty counter.
  • record(second) logs one hit at time second. Several hits can share a second.
  • recentCount(second) returns the number of hits with a time t such that second − 300 < t ≤ second, that is, the last 300 seconds including the current one.

Times are in whole seconds, and the second passed to the calls never decreases from one call to the next.

Tests are a list of operations; the first one creates the counter. The output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: At second 301 the hit from second 1 is exactly 300 seconds old and drops out. At 302 the hit from second 2 drops out too.
Three hits in one second count three times. They are still inside the window at 309 and all leave together at 310.

hints: Hits arrive in time order, and old hits only ever leave the window from the front. Which structure fits that?
Keep the times of hits in a queue. Before answering a count, what can you safely throw away for good?
In recentCount(second), drop hits from the front while their time ≤ second − 300, then return the queue length. Since time never goes back, a dropped hit is never needed again.

explain.intuition:
This is a sliding window over time. Hits enter at the back in time order, and as the clock moves forward the oldest hits fall out at the front. Since second never decreases, a hit that has left the window can never come back into it, so it can be thrown away.

A queue of hit times does exactly that. record appends; recentCount first pops every hit at or before second − 300 and then returns the size. Each hit is added once and removed at most once, so the total work is linear in the number of calls. It is the same bookkeeping a rate limiter does with a rolling window.
steps: Keep a queue of hit times and a head index (or use a real deque).
recentCount(second): while the front time is ≤ second − 300, drop it.
Return the number of times still in the queue.
pitfalls: An off-by-one at the boundary. A hit at second 1 is outside the window at second 301: the test is t ≤ second − 300 to drop.
Using array.shift() in JavaScript. It is O(n) per call; move a head index forward instead.
Collapsing hits that share a second into one entry without keeping a count. Then bursts are undercounted.

solutions.title: Keep every hit and scan
solutions.idea: Store all hit times and count the ones inside the window on each query.

solutions.title: Queue that forgets old hits
solutions.idea: Hits arrive in order and expire in order. Drop expired hits from the front before counting.

solutions.title: Sorted log and binary search
solutions.idea: Times arrive sorted, so the log is sorted. Binary-search the first time inside the window. Keeps history, which helps if old windows are queried later.

followups: A million hits arrive every second. How do 300 buckets of (second, count) keep memory fixed?
Many servers record hits at once. Where do you need locking, or how would you shard the counter?
